dolphin.title: DOLPHINS CAN SEE WITH SOUND
dolphin.script: Dolphins can build a detailed picture of the world using sound. They produce rapid clicks and listen for the echoes bouncing back from fish, rocks, and the seafloor. Those echoes reveal distance, shape, direction, and even movement. This ability is called echolocation. Dolphins also breathe consciously through a blowhole, so surfacing is an active part of life rather than an automatic reflex. They are highly social and often coordinate movement or hunting with other members of the pod. Different whistles and clicks can carry information between individuals. The strange result is an animal that can navigate dark water by turning sound into a three-dimensional map.
dolphin.caption:
Dolphins can map their surroundings with echoes. 🐬

crab.title: WHY CRABS WALK SIDEWAYS
crab.script: Many crabs are built to move sideways because the joints in their legs make lateral motion fast and stable. That helps them escape, climb over uneven ground, and move efficiently across sand or rock. Their armor is an exoskeleton worn on the outside of the body. But that shell cannot stretch, so a growing crab has to molt. The old shell splits, the crab pulls itself free, and the new shell remains soft for a short time before hardening. Some species can even regenerate a lost leg or claw over later molts. So the awkward sideways walk is actually part of a body plan that works extremely well.
crab.caption:
Crabs are built for sideways speed. 🦀
